name: Dolores "Lola" Reyes
text:
# The Spark
Light-hearted, and at your best when there is something to do.
Cheerful by disposition. Restless by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Speaks up, Open-handed, Light-hearted

## Your type
Your mood runs light, and you are at your best with something to do. A quiet week makes you restless, and a full one suits you. People catch your energy.
Where the trap is set for you: pleasure. Gregory says the enemy studies each person first, then sets the trap right next door. "pleasure borders on mirth" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like a good time: one more helping, one more episode, one more thing you enjoy a little too much.
What you bring: You make hard things feel lighter. People relax around you. You get things done.
What it costs you: You can skip past what is wrong. Pleasure can quietly become the point. Rest can feel like losing.
Kindred: Augustine, as a young man: Before his conversion he loved talk, jokes, reading together and friendly arguments. He was just as honest, later, about where his love of pleasure had led him.
Your opposite: The Deep Well (Serious by nature, and at your best when life is quiet.)

## Your leanings
- Mood: Light-hearted <-> Heavy-hearted: Light-hearted (17/100)
- Nerve: Confident <-> Careful: balanced (54/100)
- Make-up: Restless mind <-> Quiet mind: Restless mind (4/100)
- Talk: Speaks up <-> Keeps it in: Speaks up (0/100)
- Candour: Says it plainly <-> Chooses what to show: Says it plainly (33/100)
- When wronged: Lets them know <-> Lets it go: Lets it go (83/100)
- Temper: Fiery <-> Gentle: Gentle (75/100)
- Disagreements: Takes a stand <-> Keeps the peace: Keeps the peace (83/100)
- Pace: Rushes in <-> Puts it off: Rushes in (33/100)
- Follow-through: Hard to start <-> Hard to finish: Hard to start (33/100)
- Little things: Careful with little things <-> Easy on little things: balanced (42/100)
- Your own work: Sure of your work <-> Hard on yourself: balanced (50/100)
- Correction: Say it straight <-> A hint is enough: A hint is enough (75/100)
- Room: Takes up room <-> Makes yourself small: Takes up room (33/100)
- Your mind: Holds firm <-> Easily swayed: Holds firm (33/100)
- Others' wins: Simply glad <-> Feels the sting: Simply glad (17/100)
- Seen and unseen: Better in public <-> Better in private: balanced (42/100)
- After a mistake: Dwells on a mistake <-> Moves on: balanced (42/100)
- Having: Open-handed <-> Careful with what you have: Open-handed (8/100)
- Comforts: Enjoys comforts <-> Keeps a tight rein: Enjoys comforts (25/100)
Most like you: Speaks up, Open-handed, Light-hearted. Balanced: Your own work, After a mistake, Seen and unseen
* Speaks up: You think out loud, and you are easy to talk to. What you may not see: Much talk scatters the mind, Gregory says, so it loses touch with itself. And idle talk slides, step by step, into talk about other people. "it has no power to turn back within to the knowledge of itself" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Counsel: Before you speak, ask whether it is needed, or kind.
* Open-handed: You give easily. What you may not see: Gregory warns the generous against giving so much at once that they run short and start grumbling. "when the soul of the giver knows not how to endure want, then, in withdrawing much from himself, he seeks out against himself occasion of impatience" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: Give steadily and cheerfully, and do not keep score.
* Light-hearted: Your mood is light. Things rarely get you down for long. What you may not see: Gregory says pleasure sits right next door to cheerfulness. The pull you are least guarded against is the pull of a good time. Counsel: Enjoy what you are given. Keep an eye on what lives next door.

## What you might not have noticed
- You said you let rudeness go. You also said hours later you think of what you should have said. You win in the moment by staying calm. Then, on a quiet evening, it comes back bigger than it was. You can end up wishing you had been harsher than you would ever actually be. The hard part for you is not staying calm. It is the evening after. "blushes for having borne such things calmly, and is sorry that he did not return insults" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said you let things slide that you probably should not. You also said you calm things down when friends argue. Gregory says gentleness has a next-door neighbour, and it is letting things go that should not go. Keeping the peace can be love. It can also be the easier road. "Sloth is frequently looked upon as a maintenance of peace" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)

## How your anger works
Slow and brief. It takes a lot to anger you, and it does not last. Gregory says this is the one closest to peace of mind. Keep it that way. When someone wrongs you, Gregory says, remember your own faults first.

## How you speak
Words first. Words come easily, sometimes before the thought is ready. Gregory says this speaker needs holding back. The fix is simple: think first.

## How to help me
1. Ask for my help. I will give it gladly.
2. Give me room to think out loud.
3. Show me. Let me see someone do it.
4. Slow me down. I run ahead.
5. Tell me what I did well. It makes me try harder.
6. Pick the one thing that matters most, and let the rest go.
7. Tell me in private.

## Where the fight is for you now (private)
No single one leads right now. These are close, so start with the one you recognise most: Gluttony, Anger.
The first of them: Gluttony. Not eating well. Reaching for food or drink to take the edge off, or wanting something nicer than what is in front of you. Gregory says the fault is never in the food. It is in the wanting. How it talks to you: "God has created all things clean, in order to be eaten" (Gregory, Moralia on Job, gluttony’s own speech) How it shows: Eating or drinking to take the edge off. Finding it hard to stop at enough. A heavy, dull mind afterwards. What feeds it: It is natural to us, Cassian says. It can be held down but never rooted out, and it opens the door to the others. What takes its place: Cassian’s advice is steady, daily moderation, not sudden strict fasts. And break your own fast gladly for a guest.
All eight, strongest first (drawn as bars, no numbers): Gluttony, Anger, Listlessness, Pride, Vainglory, Sadness, Greed, Lust. Troubles you least: Lust.

## Your best quality, and its counterfeit
Diligence: You keep working when others stop. Counterfeit: Restlessness. Not being able to stop can feel like faithfulness. "Restlessness of spirit is frequently termed a watchful solicitude" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)

## Who you are in Christ, and in the Body
Your gladness is a gift. Kept close to God, it becomes the joy Christ promised, the kind nobody can take from you. "I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man shall take from you" (Christ, quoted by Gregory in the Pastoral Rule)
Your line: The Host (hospitality). You serve by opening your door. A meal, a bed, a welcome. People feel at home with you. Cassian names Abraham and Lot, and in his own day Macarius, who ran a guest house in Alexandria and was known as "a man of singular courtesy and patience". Second: The Watcher.
(They picked: gladly do: Have them over and cook them a meal. / Pray for them every day, without telling them.; people come for: Money, or something they need. / A place to stay, or a meal.)

# The Still Water
Careful by nature, and at your best when life is quiet.
Careful by disposition. Quiet by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Hard to start, Careful with what you have, Keeps it in

## Your type
You are careful by nature, and you are at your best when life is quiet. You see what could go wrong before most people do. A crowded week wears you down faster than it does most.
Where the trap is set for you: fear. Gregory says the enemy studies each person first, then sets the trap right next door. "Because the timid dread punishments, he threatens terrors to the fearful." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like worry. What if they are upset? What if it goes wrong? What if I say it, and it costs me?
What you bring: You see risks others miss. People trust you to be careful with them. You think best in quiet.
What it costs you: Worry can pass for wisdom. You wait to be sure, and the moment can pass. A crowded week wears you down fast.
Kindred: St Gregory the Theologian: He loved "calm and retirement" from his youth, and ran away when they made him a priest. When his best friend Basil called him lazy, he wrote back: "My greatest business always is to keep free from business." Near the end he said, "I am weary of being charged with my gentleness." | Jeremiah: When God called him, he pleaded that he was too young to speak. Gregory says he held back out of love: he longed to stay close to God in quiet. | Abba Arsenius: A desert monk who fled the world to pray. In an old story he is seen sailing in silence, with the Spirit of God beside him.
Your opposite: The Herald (Sure of yourself, and at your best when there is something to do.)

- Nerve: Confident <-> Careful: Careful (88/100)

Most like you: Hard to start, Careful with what you have, Keeps it in. Balanced: Others' wins, Temper
* Hard to start: The first step is the hardest part. What you may not see: Gregory says people who never begin are usually busy with something else they love. That has to be seen for what it is first. Counsel: Name what is holding you back. Then take one step.
* Careful with what you have: You keep a little back. What you may not see: Holding on can call itself thrift. Gregory adds that grasping often grows from fear of running short. "Tenacity is sometimes considered frugality" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Counsel: Keeping a little back can be wise. Just check whether it is wisdom or worry.
* Keeps it in: You listen more than you talk. What you may not see: The talking does not stop. It moves inside, where nobody can answer it. "more grievous loquacity in the heart" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: Your mouth needs a door, not a wall: something that opens as well as shuts.

## What you might not have noticed
- You said you listen more than you talk. You also said you have whole conversations in your head that never happen. Those are the same thing. The talking does not stop. It moves inside, where nobody can answer back. And an argument nobody can answer is easy to win. It can leave you quietly judging people who never got to reply. "For his tongue he represses, his mind he exalts" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said you let rudeness go. You also said hours later you think of what you should have said. You win in the moment by staying calm. Then, on a quiet evening, it comes back bigger than it was. You can end up wishing you had been harsher than you would ever actually be. The hard part for you is not staying calm. It is the evening after. "blushes for having borne such things calmly, and is sorry that he did not return insults" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said you hold back after a hard day. You also said you notice when other people overindulge. Gregory says self-denial has its own temptation, and it is not food. It is looking down on people who do not go without. Discipline is a gift. Judging the undisciplined is where it turns. "the pride of abstinence" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
- You said you fix things and move on. You also said you stop doing the wrong thing, but you are not one for saying sorry. Stopping is good. But Gregory says it does not undo what was done, any more than a debtor clears a debt by borrowing no more. Something still needs saying. "nor is a debtor absolved by not increasing his debt, unless he also pays what he has incurred" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)

## How your anger works
Hard wood. It takes a lot to make you angry. But once it is lit, it stays lit. It just burns where no one can see it. "others, like the heavier and harder kinds of wood, are slow in taking fire, but being once kindled, are with difficulty put out" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Gregory’s cure for your kind: say it early and calmly, before it has time to catch. And when you think about what they did, think about your own faults too.

## How you speak
Deep, but held in. You think deeply, but the words come hard. Gregory knew this speaker and did not blame them. He said they need help getting it out. Try writing it down first, or saying it to one person instead of a room.

## How to help me
1. Explain why. I need the reasons.
2. Nudge me to get started. I can be slow to begin.
3. Ask what I think. I rarely offer it.
4. Say "next time, try this", not "you did this wrong".
5. Argue it out with me. Win fairly and I will come round.
6. Tell me plainly what you need.
7. Say it straight. I can take it.

## Where the fight is for you now (private)
Right now: Greed. Not always wanting more. Often it is fear of having less. It is the grip, not the amount. Cassian says it starts with "excellent and almost reasonable excuses". How it talks to you: "It is a very blameless thing, that thou desirest some things to possess; because thou seekest not to be increased, but art afraid of being in want" (Gregory, Moralia on Job, greed’s own speech) How it shows: Finding it hard to let go of money or things, even small ones. Keeping a reserve, and never feeling it is enough. What feeds it: Gregory says sadness runs down into it: a heart with no joy inside looks for comfort in owning things. What takes its place: Cassian says cut the desire, not only the spending. Be content with what you need.
All eight, strongest first (drawn as bars, no numbers): Greed, Listlessness, Pride, Sadness, Anger, Gluttony, Lust, Vainglory. Troubles you least: Vainglory.

## Your best quality, and its counterfeit
Thrift: You take care of what you have been given. Counterfeit: Holding on. Tightness can call itself good sense. "niggardliness palliates itself under the name of frugality" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
Your strength: Counsel. Its partner: Courage. You think it through well. The risk is that you never get round to doing it.

## Who you are in Christ, and in the Body
Your care is a gift. Gregory says the fearful should not stay in fear but grow, fed by love, until love does what fear used to do. "grow up by the nursing of charity to the grace of love" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
Your line: The Teacher (teaching). You serve by helping people understand. You explain, you make it clear, you pass it on. Cassian names people who "give themselves up to teaching" as one of the lines God gives. Second: The Giver.
(They picked: gladly do: Quietly pay for something they can’t afford. / Explain something until they finally understand it.; people come for: Someone to take charge and sort things out. / Something explained or taught.)

# The Deep Well
Serious by nature, and at your best when life is quiet.
Serious by disposition. Quiet by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Holds firm, Keeps a tight rein, Heavy-hearted

## Your type
You are serious by nature, and you are at your best when life is quiet. You feel things deeply and think them through. People come to you when something really matters.
Where the trap is set for you: a quarrel. Gregory says the enemy studies each person first, then sets the trap right next door. "And because moroseness easily slides into anger, he offers the cup of discord for the morose." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like being right about how badly you have been treated.
What you bring: You take people and things seriously. You are honest about sorrow. You think best in quiet.
What it costs you: Hurts go deep and stay. Heaviness can turn into irritation. A crowded week wears you down fast.
Kindred: St Gregory the Great: The man whose book this quiz is built on. He opens his Dialogues alone in a place he says suited "a sad and melancholy disposition", and he wrote that he loved the quiet life and had the busy one forced on him. | Elijah: After his great victory on Carmel he ran into the wilderness and sat under a tree. "I have had enough, LORD," he said. The desert fathers remembered him as the one who "loved silence".
Your opposite: The Spark (Light-hearted, and at your best when there is something to do.)
Close call: your make-up is balanced; you could also be The Forge.

- Nerve: Confident <-> Careful: Careful (75/100)
- Make-up: Restless mind <-> Quiet mind: balanced (58/100)

* Holds firm: Once you decide, you stay decided. What you may not see: Gregory says stubbornness often passes for constancy, and grows from thinking a little too much of our own judgment. Counsel: Take good advice, even when it was not your idea.
* Keeps a tight rein: You hold yourself back. What you may not see: Gregory says the self-denying are not tempted by food. They are tempted by pride in going without, and by impatience with people who do not. "the pride of abstinence" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Counsel: Give away what you go without, and do not judge the one who eats.
* Heavy-hearted: You feel things heavily, and they stay. What you may not see: Gregory says heaviness slides easily into irritation, and from there into quarrels. "moroseness easily slides into anger" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Counsel: Watch for bitterness that calls itself honesty.

## What you might not have noticed
- You said you hold back after a hard day. You also said you notice when other people overindulge. Gregory says self-denial has its own temptation, and it is not food. It is looking down on people who do not go without. Discipline is a gift. Judging the undisciplined is where it turns. "the pride of abstinence" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
- You said you listen more than you talk. You also said you have whole conversations in your head that never happen. Those are the same thing. The talking does not stop. It moves inside, where nobody can answer back. And an argument nobody can answer is easy to win. It can leave you quietly judging people who never got to reply. "For his tongue he represses, his mind he exalts" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said you tell people in charge when they are wrong. You also said your anger usually feels justified. Gregory would call that a pair. What feels like honesty can be pride, and what feels like zeal can be temper. Neither means you are wrong. It means the feeling of being right is not proof. "they think the goad of their anger to be the zeal of righteousness" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said things stay with you for a while. You also said once you are angry, it can last for days. Gregory saw the link. A heavy heart slides easily into anger, and a slow anger turns into a grudge. They feed each other. "And because moroseness easily slides into anger, he offers the cup of discord for the morose." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)

## How your anger works
Quick and lasting. Your anger catches fast and stays long. Gregory did not soften it: of the four, he calls this the worst. It is also the one where a little work changes the most. "Others again, and their conduct is the worst, are both quick in catching the flames of anger, and slow in letting them go" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Gregory gives two cures. Before the day starts, think through what might go wrong, so nothing catches you asleep. And when someone wrongs you, remember your own faults.

## How you speak
Full in both. You think things through, and the words come easily. Gregory calls this speaker "worthy of praise". The gift is meant to be used for others.

## How to help me
1. Show me. Let me see someone do it.
2. Give me time to come round. Pressure makes me dig in.
3. Ask what I think. I rarely offer it.
4. Be specific about what could be better.
5. Say "next time, try this", not "you did this wrong".

## Where the fight is for you now (private)
No single one leads right now. These are close, so start with the one you recognise most: Sadness, Pride.
The first of them: Sadness. A heavy sorrow. Cassian says there are two kinds. One comes after anger has died down, or after a loss. The other comes from unreasonable anxiety. How it talks to you: "What ground hast thou to rejoice, when thou endurest so many wrongs from thy neighbours?" (Gregory, Moralia on Job, sadness’s own speech) How it shows: The people you love come round, and everything they say seems badly timed. Or a flat heaviness you cannot explain. What feeds it: Cassian says one kind follows anger or a loss, and the other comes from anxiety. If anger is feeding yours, deal with the anger and this weakens. What takes its place: Not cheerfulness. Cassian says its place is taken by "a godly sorrow and one full of joy".
All eight, strongest first (drawn as bars, no numbers): Sadness, Pride, Anger, Listlessness, Greed, Gluttony, Lust, Vainglory. Troubles you least: Vainglory.

## Your best quality, and its counterfeit
Self-control: You can say no to yourself. Counterfeit: Pride in going without. Self-denial can become something to be proud of. "the pride of abstinence" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
Your strength: Counsel. Its partner: Courage. You think it through well. The risk is that you never get round to doing it.

## Who you are in Christ, and in the Body
Your seriousness is not a flaw to be fixed. Held under reason, the fire in it becomes holy zeal. "For some are possessed by anger, but while they submit this to reason, they convert it into service rendered to holy zeal." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
Your line: The Watcher (prayer and quiet). You serve by praying. Quietly, faithfully, often unseen. The Church has always needed people who keep watch while others work. Cassian names this line first: people who seek "purity of heart" in silence, like Elijah and Elisha, and St Antony in his own day. Second: The Giver.

You can end up wishing you had been harsher than you would ever actually be. The hard part for you is not staying calm. It is the evening after. - You said you hold back after a hard day. You also said you notice when other people overindulge. Gregory says self-denial has its own temptation, and it is not food. - You said things stay with you for a while. You also said once you are angry, it can last for days. Gregory saw the link. - You said your gut says “let me think” when a friend asks for money. You also said you find it hard to let go of money or things. ## How your anger works
Quick and lasting. Your anger catches fast and stays long. Gregory did not soften it: of the four, he calls this the worst. It is also the one where a little work changes the most. Deep, but held in. You think deeply, but the words come hard. Gregory knew this speaker and did not blame them. He said they need help getting it out. Try writing it down first, or saying it to one person instead of a room.

2. Tell me in private.
3. Give me time to come round. Pressure makes me dig in.
4. Say "next time, try this", not "you did this wrong".

Your strength: Counsel. Its partner: Courage. You think it through well. The risk is that you never get round to doing it.

* Keeps the peace: You calm things down. What you may not see: Gregory warns the peaceable not to love peace so much that they never tell anyone they are wrong. - You said people you have just met get your best. You also said you care what people think of you. Those are one thing. The good you do in public is real. "to know how sometimes to be silent about what is true" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: Keep your honesty. Choose your moment.
* Takes a stand: You say where you stand. What you may not see: Gregory says many quarrels grow from pride in a gift that sets us apart, like knowing more or trying harder. Counsel: Win the point without losing the person.
* Hard to start: The first step is the hardest part. What you may not see: Gregory says people who never begin are usually busy with something else they love. That has to be seen for what it is first. Counsel: Name what is holding you back. Then take one step.

## What you might not have noticed
- You said you let people know on the spot. You also said you snap, and wish you had not. Gregory saw this exactly. Anger drives you somewhere you never meant to go, and you only see it when it is over. It is not that you do not care. It is that the care arrives too late. "fury drives the mind whither desire draws it not" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said you tell people in charge when they are wrong. You also said your anger usually feels justified. Gregory would call that a pair. What feels like honesty can be pride, and what feels like zeal can be temper. Neither means you are wrong. It means the feeling of being right is not proof. "they think the goad of their anger to be the zeal of righteousness" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)

## How your anger works
Kindled reeds. Your anger flares and fades. You would probably say you rarely hold a grudge. Ask someone close to you whether they agree. The danger is the first minute: what you say before it burns out. "like kindled reeds, while they clamour with their voices, give out something like a crackle at their kindling" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Gregory’s cure for your kind: when someone wrongs you, remember your own faults first. It takes the heat out of the first minute.

## How you speak
Full in both. You think things through, and the words come easily. Gregory calls this speaker "worthy of praise". The gift is meant to be used for others.

## How to help me
1. Nudge me to get started. I can be slow to begin.
2. Say it straight. I can take it.
3. Be specific about what could be better.

## Where the fight is for you now (private)
No single one leads right now. These are close, so start with the one you recognise most: Gluttony, Listlessness.
The first of them: Gluttony. Not eating well. Reaching for food or drink to take the edge off, or wanting something nicer than what is in front of you. Gregory says the fault is never in the food. It is in the wanting. How it talks to you: "God has created all things clean, in order to be eaten" (Gregory, Moralia on Job, gluttony’s own speech) How it shows: Eating or drinking to take the edge off. Finding it hard to stop at enough. A heavy, dull mind afterwards. What feeds it: It is natural to us, Cassian says. It can be held down but never rooted out, and it opens the door to the others. What takes its place: Cassian’s advice is steady, daily moderation, not sudden strict fasts. And break your own fast gladly for a guest.
All eight, strongest first (drawn as bars, no numbers): Gluttony, Listlessness, Greed, Pride, Anger, Sadness, Lust, Vainglory. Troubles you least: Vainglory.

## Your best quality, and its counterfeit
Glad admiration: Other people’s good makes you happy. Counterfeit: Watching from the stands. Admiring can take the place of trying. "eager backers, but inert spectators" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
Your strength: Counsel. Its partner: Courage. You think it through well. The risk is that you never get round to doing it.

## Who you are in Christ, and in the Body
Your gladness is a gift. Kept close to God, it becomes the joy Christ promised, the kind nobody can take from you. "I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man shall take from you" (Christ, quoted by Gregory in the Pastoral Rule)
Your line: The Teacher (teaching). You serve by helping people understand. You explain, you make it clear, you pass it on. Cassian names people who "give themselves up to teaching" as one of the lines God gives. Second: The Host.
(They picked: gladly do: Have them over and cook them a meal. / Explain something until they finally understand it.; people come for: Something explained or taught. / Someone to take charge and sort things out.)

# The Hearth
Light-hearted, and at your best when life is quiet.
Cheerful by disposition. Quiet by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Simply glad, Open-handed, Enjoys comforts

## Your type
Your mood runs light, and you are at your best when life is quiet. You enjoy things as they come: a meal, a long talk, an evening at home. People tend to relax around you.
Where the trap is set for you: pleasure. Gregory says the enemy studies each person first, then sets the trap right next door. "pleasure borders on mirth" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like a good time: one more helping, one more episode, one more thing you enjoy a little too much.
What you bring: You make hard things feel lighter. People relax around you. You think best in quiet.
What it costs you: You can skip past what is wrong. Pleasure can quietly become the point. A crowded week wears you down fast.
Kindred: St Antony the Great: He spent twenty years alone in the desert. When he came out, Athanasius says, his friends were amazed at how settled he was, and his face was cheerful because his soul was at peace.
Your opposite: The Forge (Serious by nature, and at your best when there is something to do.)

- Little things: Careful with little things <-> Easy on little things: Careful with little things (33/100)

- Having: Open-handed <-> Careful with what you have: Open-handed (17/100)
- Comforts: Enjoys comforts <-> Keeps a tight rein: Enjoys comforts (25/100)

"when the soul of the giver knows not how to endure want, then, in withdrawing much from himself, he seeks out against himself occasion of impatience" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: Give steadily and cheerfully, and do not keep score.

"Sloth is frequently looked upon as a maintenance of peace" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
